title: Role of __name__ == __main__
prompt_markdown: What is the standard purpose of `if __name__ == "__main__":` in a Python script?

choices: It defines the primary class of an object-oriented file.
It prevents code from executing when the file is imported as a module by another script.
It enforces Python type checking during module compilation.
It optimizes module loading speed by caching bytecode in __pycache__.
content.explanation: When a file is run directly, `__name__` is set to `"__main__"`. When imported into another module, `__name__` is the module name, allowing scripts to provide reusable functions without running CLI commands upon import.

title: Python sys.path and imports
prompt_markdown: Where does Python look first when executing an `import my_module` statement?
hints: Think about built-in modules vs filesystem.

choices: In `sys.modules` (already loaded modules cache), then built-in modules, then directories in `sys.path`.
In the global site-packages directory exclusively.
On PyPI via an internet lookup.
content.explanation: Python checks `sys.modules` cache first. If absent, it checks built-in modules, and then searches directories listed in `sys.path` (starting with the directory of the running script).

title: Circular Imports Problem and Solutions
prompt_markdown: What causes a circular import error in Python, and what are two architectural techniques to resolve it?
hints: Module A imports B, while module B imports A.

rubric: Explains that module A imports B while B simultaneously imports A during module initialization.
Provides at least two remediation methods: refactoring shared types/functions into a third module, importing inside a function/method, or using typing.TYPE_CHECKING.
content.reference_answer: A circular import occurs when Module A imports Module B at top-level, while Module B also imports Module A, creating a deadlock where one module is accessed before its attributes are defined. Remediation techniques include: 1) Extracting shared models or utilities into a separate common module (e.g. `models.py` or `constants.py`); 2) Moving the import statement inside the specific function or method where it is used; 3) Using `from typing import TYPE_CHECKING` so the import only occurs during static analysis, not runtime.

title: __init__.py in Modern Python
prompt_markdown: What is the role of `__init__.py` in Python packages, and why is it still recommended in professional codebases despite implicit namespace packages?
hints: PEP 420 introduced namespace packages, but __init__.py defines public API export.

rubric: Explains that __init__.py marks a directory as a regular Python package.
Explains its role in defining package-level public APIs via __all__ and explicit re-exports.
Mentions that tools (linters, pytest, typecheckers) rely on it for root detection.
content.reference_answer: Although Python 3.3+ supports namespace packages without `__init__.py`, including an explicit `__init__.py` is best practice because: 1) It serves as the package entry point to define clean public exports (using `__all__` or exposing key classes so users can write `from pkg import Model` instead of deep internal paths); 2) Static analysis tools, IDEs, and test runners like pytest use it to unambiguously determine package roots and module hierarchies.
